title: Strobogrammatic Number
description: Brute force to optimized: constructing the fully rotated string and comparing it versus a two-pointer check that verifies rotated digit pairs directly.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string num representing an integer, return true if num is strobogrammatic, meaning it looks the same when rotated 180 degrees (looked at upside down).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Determine whether flipping num upside down (rotating the whole string 180 degrees) produces the exact same string back.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Number Printed on Both Sides of a Coin
blocks.text: Picture a number stamped on a coin, and turning the coin upside down to see if it reads the exact same number. Only some digits (0, 1, 6, 8, 9) even remain readable digits when flipped, and 6 becomes 9 (and vice versa) rather than staying the same.

blocks.caption: Only 0, 1, 6, 8, 9 survive a 180-degree rotation, and 6 and 9 swap with each other

blocks.text: Rotated 180 degrees, "69" becomes "69" again: the 6 becomes a 9 and moves to the other end, and the 9 becomes a 6 and moves to the first end, reproducing the original string.
The digit 2 has no valid rotated form, so the string cannot be strobogrammatic.
Before literally constructing the rotated string and comparing it to the original, notice that checking digit pairs directly, from both ends inward, avoids ever building a new string.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Rotating the whole string 180 degrees both rotates each individual digit AND reverses their order (the last digit becomes the first, rotated).

Observation 2: This means the digit at position i must, when rotated, equal the ORIGINAL digit at the mirrored position from the end.

Observation 3: A lookup table mapping each valid digit to its rotated form (0 to 0, 1 to 1, 6 to 9, 8 to 8, 9 to 6) makes each individual check O(1).

Observation 4: Walking two pointers inward from both ends, checking this pairing at each step, verifies the whole string without ever constructing a rotated copy.
This leads to a two-pointer check from both ends of the string, verifying at each step that the digit pairing matches the rotation rules.
Construct the fully rotated string by rotating and reversing every digit, then compare it directly to the original.

items: For each digit in num, look up its rotated equivalent (or fail if it has none).
Reverse the order of the rotated digits to build the fully rotated string.
Compare the rotated string to the original num.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build the entire rotated string, then compare it to the original

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every digit is individually rotated and collected, then the whole collected sequence is reversed to represent the physical 180-degree flip.
The fully rotated string is materialized before being compared to the original.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), where n is the string length.
Space: O(n), for the constructed rotated string.
Limitation: building an entirely new string just to compare it to the original uses extra space that a direct two-pointer comparison would avoid.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why constructing the rotated string is unnecessary: the comparison being performed is really just checking, for each position, whether the digit there rotates into the digit at the mirrored position, which can be checked directly without ever materializing a new string.

What the two-pointer check verifies: starting from both ends and moving inward, at each step, the left digit's rotated form must equal the right digit.

The core idea: walk two pointers inward from both ends, checking the pairing rule directly at each step, with no extra string built.

Use two pointers, one starting at the beginning and one at the end of num. At each step, look up the left digit's rotated form and check it against the right digit; if it does not match (or the left digit has no valid rotated form), return false immediately. Move both pointers inward and repeat until they meet or cross.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: check rotated digit pairs directly from both ends, no new string built

blocks.text: Since a 180-degree rotation both rotates each digit and reverses the string's order, checking the digit at position i against the rotated digit at the mirrored position from the end, moving inward from both ends, verifies exactly the same condition a full rotate-and-compare would, without ever constructing a new string.

blocks.text: This problem is a straightforward two-pointer check once the rotation-pair lookup table is known; the only real insight is recognizing that a full rotation combines digit-level rotation with string-level reversal, both handled together by comparing from opposite ends inward.

items: Forgetting that 6 and 9 rotate into EACH OTHER, not into themselves.
Not rejecting digits like 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, which have no valid rotated form at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single-digit string like \"0\", \"1\", or \"8\"","true, these digits rotate into themselves."],["An odd-length string with a non-self-rotating middle digit (like 6 or 9)","false, the middle digit must rotate into itself when centered."]]}

blocks.text: Stating the rotation lookup table explicitly, and noting that a full rotation reverses order as well as rotating digits, clarifies why the two-pointer approach correctly mirrors a true 180-degree flip.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid building the rotated string", think: check the pairing directly with two pointers moving inward from both ends.

items: How would you generate all strobogrammatic numbers of a given length, rather than just checking one?
How would this check change if uppercase letters that also look rotationally symmetric (like the digit-letter mappings in some variants) were included?
Valid Palindrome and other two-pointer symmetric-check problems, though here the check is a rotation mapping instead of plain equality.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(n) time; the brute force uses O(n) space to build the rotated string, while the optimized two-pointer check uses O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: two-pointer symmetric check using a rotation-pair lookup table.
Core Idea: check each digit against its rotated form at the mirrored position, from both ends inward, without ever constructing a rotated copy of the string.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized two-pointer check.
Most Important Observation: a 180-degree rotation both rotates individual digits and reverses their order, both handled at once by comparing from opposite ends.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the rotation lookup table is known.
One line memory trick: two pointers inward, checking that each digit rotates into its mirrored partner.
